newsitem.title: CANADA: Wheat prices appear to have bottomed - CWB analyst.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices appear to have bottomed - CWB analyst.

text.p: World wheat prices appeared to bottom out two weeks ago as export demand rose and attention turned to dry conditions in Australia, a Canadian Wheat Board market analyst told Reuters.

"You could say that it looks like wheat prices bottomed out a couple of weeks ago and that it could be recovering but with the caveat that the USDA is still projecting very large world wheat production," CWB analyst Peter Watts said.
Wheat prices appeared to bottom out on July 7 when Chicago Board of Trade September closed at US$3.21-3/4 a bushel.
The CBOT September wheat futures closed at US$3.58-1/2 on Thursday, an 11.4 percent recovery since July 7.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture on July 11 pegged world wheat output in 1997/98 (June/July) at 587 million tonnes.
That would be the world's second largest crop after the record set in 1990/91 at 588 million tonnes and above the projection for 1996/97 at 583 million tonnes, Watts said.

While world supply was expected to trend up, output among four of the five major exporters was likely to decline or remain unchanged with only the United States likely to produce four million more tonnes, Watts said.
"Australia's been very dry. If it remains dry for the next two weeks, you'll see reductions in production," Watts said.

Canadian production may decline five million tonnes in 1997/98 compared to 1996/97, Australian output could drop five to seven million tonnes and Argentine wheat production may fall two million tonnes, Watts said.
European output was likely to remain unchanged, he said.
Meanwhile, import demand appeared to pick up recently.
"Egypt bought 200,000 tonnes of soft red winter wheat this week so that's changed the psychology of the market a little bit," Watts said.
"Any kind of news like the drought in Australia, the big buy from Egypt, Pakistan is tendering today for 500,000 tonnes of wheat, can turn the market around pretty quick," he added.
Although China, a major importer, may have record output with the USDA forecasting a 114 million tonne crop, other buyers should make up the difference, he said.
"Psychologically China has an important impact on the market despite the fact that really, Iran, Egypt and Japan are far more important importers than China this year," he said.
